paras: The killing of Dick Bross was the fatal shooting of Richard "Dick" Bross, a Black man, by John Orr, a white deck-hand, in a basement tenement at 394 Clark Street, Chicago, on the night of August 28, 1880. Orr and Frank Gilbert, a Black man who had been with him, were arrested, and a coroner's jury held Orr as principal and Gilbert as accessory to murder. The Chicago Tribune followed the case for three days, and a wire dispatch carried it east as the murder of a "colored man" by a white man.

The basement lay in a district called "Cheyenne," under a saloon, in a building the Tribune said was let to "negroes and low whites." The Tribune described Bross as about 45, born a slave in the South, and a former stevedore. Orr said he was a deck-hand on the propeller Fremont on a spree ashore, and Gilbert had left the Joliet penitentiary less than three weeks before.

Earlier that evening Bross, by Orr's account, "made some talk," and Gilbert later told Orr that Bross had drawn a razor on him. Orr said he gave Gilbert money for a revolver, bought cartridges, and went back with him "to see if Bross would cut us then." Residents said Gilbert had meanwhile warned Bross that the white man meant to shoot him, but Bross refused to leave, saying he had done nothing to be afraid of.

About 9 p.m. Bross was shot in the right breast in the basement hall. At the inquest Louisa Lewis testified that Orr accused Bross of having a razor, Bross denied it, and Orr shot him in the scuffle, after which Gilbert grabbed the revolver and ran. Several Black men from the neighborhood seized Orr, and Thomas Scott held him until Officers Dollard and Holland took him to the station. Asked who shot him, Bross answered, "Jack Orr, I think. He was a white man," and he died soon after reaching the hospital.

Police found Gilbert within minutes on Fourth Avenue; Orr denied firing and pointed to Gilbert, who said he had been two blocks away. Three residents were held as witnesses, and the next morning police "pulled" the den and sheltered its occupants at the Armory. On August 30 Coroner Mann's jury heard thirteen witnesses and held Orr to the grand jury as principal and Gilbert as accessory, and both were booked into adjoining cells on "murderers' row." No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage, which ends on August 31.

The Chicago Tribune headlined its first account "Another Murder," blaming "Bad Whisky and a Depraved Woman." Its reporter, who said he was across the street at the shot, spent much of the story on the tenement, calling its residents "depraved creatures" and the basement "almost as impenetrable to the civilized white as an African jungle." Yet the same report rejected the razor story, said Bross "never acted like" a bad man, and named Orr "beyond all doubt" the murderer. Later the paper shifted blame to Gilbert, calling Orr "simply the tool of the negro" and the killing "a premeditated murder in the fullest sense of the term" for which hanging was possible.

Outside Chicago, the dispatch ran on August 30 in the New-York Tribune, the New York Sun and the Washington National Republican, under headlines from "A Colored Man Murdered" to "A Cold-Blooded Murder." News summaries in Lancaster, Delaware and Maine papers repeated it, the Delaware Daily Republican saying Bross was "deliberately murdered" over a quarrel.

Accounts differed over who fired: Orr denied it, the Tribune reported that some believed Gilbert had, and inquest witnesses put the revolver in Orr's hand. The motive was given variously as an earlier quarrel, Gilbert's razor story, which witnesses called a lie, and, according to Lou Watts and the Tribune, Gilbert's jealousy of Bross.

reader.title: Killing of Dick Bross
bases: A single white man, with a Black companion later held as accessory, shot a Black man after a quarrel in a tenement basement; no mob, band or officers were involved and no racial motive is stated (A1, A9).

The Chicago Tribune's local reporting (A1, A3), the coroner's jury verdict it reported (A9), and a separate Chicago wire dispatch (A2, A4, A5) agree that Orr shot and killed Bross at 394 Clark Street.

accounts.label: Orr's statement
accounts.gist: Orr said Gilbert told him Bross drew a razor on him, that he gave Gilbert money for a revolver and bought cartridges, and that they went back to the basement; he denied firing and pointed to Gilbert, who was behind him.

accounts.label: Gilbert's statement
accounts.gist: Gilbert said he was with Orr when the revolver was bought and heard him say he would shoot Bross, but left when the quarrel began and was two blocks away at the shot.

accounts.label: Residents held as witnesses
accounts.gist: Bross may have talked brashly but the razor story was Gilbert's lie; Gilbert had warned Bross the white man meant to shoot him, and Bross refused to leave.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury testimony
accounts.gist: Louisa Lewis and Maggie Moore said Orr accused Bross of having a razor, Bross denied it, and Orr shot him in the scuffle while Gilbert grabbed the revolver and fled; the jury held Orr as principal and Gilbert as accessory.

accounts.label: Chicago wire report
accounts.gist: After trouble earlier in the evening, Orr went out, bought a pistol, returned and shot Bross through the right breast; Orr was arrested.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune called the killing murder and Orr the murderer, and said Bross 'never acted like' a bad man, while blaming 'Bad Whisky and a Depraved Woman' and describing the tenement's Black and white residents as 'depraved creatures' in an 'African jungle.'
After the inquest the Chicago Tribune called it 'a premeditated murder in the fullest sense of the term,' concocted by Gilbert, and noted that hanging was possible.
Eastern papers ran the Chicago dispatch under 'A Colored Man Murdered,' 'Murder in Chicago' and 'A Cold-Blooded Murder,' locating it in 'one of the lowest portions of the city.'

versions.value: Orr fired the revolver in a scuffle (inquest witnesses; Tribune's first report)
Orr denied firing and implied Gilbert, who was behind him
Some thought Gilbert and not Orr fired the shot

conflicts.note: Sworn inquest testimony and the coroner's verdict name Orr as principal; the Gilbert version rests on Orr's denial and unattributed opinion.

conflicts.note: The Tribune's view shifted over three days; the coroner's jury held Gilbert as accessory.

John Orr (white deck-hand), held as principal; Frank Gilbert (Black), held as accessory.
Individuals (one shooter and an alleged accomplice); no mob or officers.

record_check.record: John Orr, a white sailor, shot and killed Dick (Richard) Bross, a Black man, in a Clark Street basement dive in Chicago; Orr was arrested.
record_check.dossier: Accurate but omits Gilbert, his arrest and the coroner's jury holding Orr as principal and Gilbert as accessory.
